summary.text: Digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble food compounds into small water-soluble components that can be absorbed into the blood plasma.
It comes in two kinds: mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, while chemical digestion uses enzymes to break food into compounds the body can use.
In humans it starts in the mouth with chewing and saliva, continues in the stomach with gastric juice, and goes on in the small intestine, where 95% of nutrient absorption occurs.

items.explain: Mechanical digestion is the physical breakdown of large pieces of food into smaller pieces, and chewing is a form of it.

items.prompt: The stomach holds strong hydrochloric acid, yet its own wall is not eaten away. What protects it?

options.label: A thick coat of saliva swallowed with food
Pepsin neutralizing the acid
Bile released from the liver
A slimy layer of mucus and bicarbonates

items.explain: Mucus and bicarbonates secreted by the stomach form a slimy shield against chemicals like concentrated hydrochloric acid.

items.prompt: A person eats a chicken breast. Where does digestion of its protein begin, and what starts it?

options.label: In the mouth, with amylase in saliva
In the large intestine, with bacteria
In the stomach, with gastric juice containing pepsin
In the rectum, with bile

items.explain: Gastric juice in the stomach starts protein digestion, and it mainly contains hydrochloric acid and pepsin.

items.prompt: Partly digested food leaves the stomach when a valve opens. What does it meet next in the duodenum?

options.label: Saliva from the salivary glands and more gastric juice
Enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver
Mucus from the mouth and acid from the liver
Pepsin from the pancreas and amylase from the liver

items.explain: In the duodenum the chyme mixes with digestive enzymes from the pancreas and bile juice from the liver.

items.prompt: Most fungi digest food very differently from humans. How?

options.label: They release enzymes outside the body and absorb what diffuses back
They swallow food and break it down in a stomach
They chew food with teeth before absorbing it
They wait for bacteria to digest it inside them

items.explain: In external digestion, enzymes are secreted into the surroundings and break down material there, and some products diffuse back; most fungi still rely on it.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking food down
paragraphs.text: Digestion is the work of turning large food compounds that do not dissolve in water into small ones that do. Being small and soluble lets them be absorbed into the blood plasma. The process is usually split in two, depending on how the food gets broken apart. Mechanical digestion physically breaks big pieces into smaller ones, which digestive enzymes can then reach. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to split food into the small compounds the body can use.

paragraphs.heading: It starts in the mouth
paragraphs.text: In people, digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing, called mastication, breaks food up and saliva wets it. Saliva comes from the salivary glands and carries an enzyme, salivary amylase, that starts breaking down starch. It also holds mucus to make food slippery, and hydrogencarbonate (HCO⁻₃), which sets the right pH for amylase to do its work. About 30% of the starch is already broken down in the mouth, and by then the chewed food has become a small, round, soft mass called a bolus. Studies suggest that chewing each bite more times raises relevant gut hormones and may lower how hungry people say they feel and how much they eat.

paragraphs.heading: Acid and churning in the stomach
paragraphs.text: Peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction, pushes the bolus down the esophagus into the stomach. There gastric juice, made mostly of hydrochloric acid and pepsin, starts digesting protein, and the acid supplies an acidic pH for pepsin. Since the acid and pepsin could harm the stomach wall, the stomach also releases mucus and bicarbonates, which form a slimy shield that also helps lubrication. Meanwhile peristalsis keeps mixing the food so it blends further with the enzymes.

paragraphs.heading: The small intestine finishes
paragraphs.text: When a valve called the pyloric sphincter opens, the partly digested food, now called chyme, moves into the duodenum. There it mixes with enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver, and digestion carries on through the small intestine. Pepsin has already cut proteins into peptides or proteoses, and enzymes in the small intestine break these into dipeptides and amino acids. Fully digested chyme passes through the liver before it is absorbed into the blood, and 95% of nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine.

paragraphs.heading: Last stops
paragraphs.text: Some absorption happens elsewhere. The stomach takes in some water, simple sugar and alcohol. In the colon, or large intestine, water and minerals return to the blood in slightly acidic conditions, with a pH of about 5.6 to 6.9. Bacteria in the colon make some vitamins, such as biotin and vitamin K, which are absorbed there too. What is left, the feces, leaves the body from the rectum during defecation.

paragraphs.heading: Outside or inside the body
paragraphs.text: Across living things digestion takes many forms, but a basic split is between external and internal digestion. External digestion appeared earlier in evolution, and most fungi still use it: they release enzymes into their surroundings, the enzymes break down organic material, and some of the products diffuse back. Animals instead digest inside a tube, the gastrointestinal tract. That is more efficient, since more of the broken-down products are captured and the chemical conditions inside are easier to control. Nearly all spiders release toxins and digestive chemicals outside their bodies first, and then take in the resulting soup.
